a: The Simon already mentioned
p: The quarrel of chapter 3 goes on: Simon, a temple officer, now slanders the high priest.
b: Simon was "of the tribe of Benjamin" and "overseer of the temple" (3:4). After quarreling with the high priest Onias III over the city market, he told the Seleucid governor that the temple treasury held great wealth (3:4–6), which brought Heliodorus to Jerusalem. Now that Heliodorus has failed, Simon turns the blame on Onias. His brother is Menelaus (4:23), so this rivalry runs through the whole crisis: a family outside the line of high priests against the house of Onias.

a: had stirred things up with Heliodorus
p: The Greek verb can mean that Onias struck Heliodorus, or that he set him on to make trouble.
b: The verb episeiō means "to shake (something) at" someone. Simon's charge may be that Onias had Heliodorus beaten (the flogging of 3:26 was done by heavenly figures, but Simon could claim men did it), or that Onias "incited" Heliodorus in the first place. The KJV took it a third way, "terrified". The Plain keeps a wording that leaves the question open. Either way the slander turns the story of 3:24–30 upside down, making God's rescue of the temple into the high priest's plot.
orig: τὸν Ἡλιόδωρον ἐπισεσεικὼς (ton Hēliodōron episeseikōs)

a: the man who did good to the city
p: Euergetēs was the honor Greek cities gave their patrons; the writer gives it to Onias.
b: Greek cities set up inscriptions to their euergetai, "benefactors", and kings took the word as a title (Ptolemy III Euergetes). The writer gives Onias the honors of a Greek civic patron: benefactor of the city, protector of his people, zealous for the laws. In a book written in polished Greek, the faithful high priest is the true model citizen, and his enemies are the bad ones. Jesus mocks the same title: rulers "are called benefactors" (Luke 22:25).
orig: τὸν εὐεργέτην τῆς πόλεως (ton euergetēn tēs poleōs)

a: He went not as an accuser of his fellow citizens
p: Onias appeals to the Seleucid king. The writer defends him from the charge of informing on his people.
b: Going over a local quarrel to the king could look like betrayal, and the writer takes care to say it was not. Onias sought "what would benefit the whole people". The book does not object to Seleucid rule as such: its good times are when kings honor the temple (3:1–3). Onias's trip to Antioch also explains why he is there, and not in Jerusalem, when his brother takes his office (4:7) and when he is murdered near Antioch (4:33–34).

a: Seleucus departed this life
p: Seleucus IV was murdered in 175 BC. His brother Antiochus IV took the throne.
b: Seleucus IV Philopator was killed in 175 BC in a plot led by the same Heliodorus who appears in chapter 3; the Roman historian Appian tells of it (Syrian Wars 45). His brother Antiochus, back from years as a hostage in Rome (1 Maccabees 1:10), seized the throne, at first as guardian of the dead king's young son. He took the title Epiphanes, "God made manifest"; Polybius reports that people called him Epimanes, "the madman", for his behavior (Polybius 26.1a, quoted by Athenaeus). The writer uses "departed this life" (metallaxantos ton bion), and the same verb returns for the martyrs' deaths (6:31; 7:7).

a: Jason, Onias's brother
p: Josephus says Jason's Hebrew name was Jesus (Joshua). His account of these high priests differs from this book's.
b: Josephus says the high priest's brother "Jesus changed his name to Jason" (Antiquities 12.239), a Greek name that sounds like the Hebrew. But Josephus tells the story differently. In his account Jason takes office after Onias has died, Onias's son is still a child, and Menelaus is a third brother, also named Onias (12.237–239). 2 Maccabees, closer to the events, makes Menelaus a brother of Simon the Benjaminite (4:23), and has Onias alive until about 170 BC. Most historians prefer 2 Maccabees here.

a: crept into the high priesthood by underhanded means
p: The verb means to get something by fraud, as a forger passes off false coin. Here a high priest buys his office.
b: Hyponotheuō means to get something by underhand or illegitimate means, from nothos, "bastard, counterfeit". The book uses the word again when Menelaus outbids Jason (4:26). Until now the high priesthood had passed from father to son in Onias's family, the line of Zadok, and the king confirmed it. Jason was of that family, but he took his brother's place by paying the king. Menelaus, who was not of that family, would do the same. 1 Maccabees mentions none of this, though it later notes high priests named by kings (1 Maccabees 7:9; 1 Maccabees 10:20).
orig: ὑπενόθευσεν Ἰάσων ὁ ἀδελφὸς Ὀνίου τὴν ἀρχιερωσύνην (hypenotheusen Iasōn ho adelphos Oniou tēn archierōsynēn)

a: three hundred sixty talents of silver
p: Jason offered 440 talents, probably each year, plus 150 for the gymnasium. Menelaus bid 300 more.
b: A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kg) of silver. Jason's bid of 360 + 80 talents, plus 150 for his reform, is high. The Seleucids were short of money: since the Peace of Apamea (188 BC) they owed Rome a huge war payment, and Seleucus IV had already looked to the Jerusalem treasury (chapter 3). Historians take the bids as yearly tribute. 1 Maccabees 11:28 records Jonathan's offer of three hundred talents to Demetrius II for tax relief, a similar sum.

a: a gymnasium and a training corps for youths
p: The gymnasium trained a city's young men in sport and Greek culture; the ephebate was its corps of young citizens.
b: In a Greek city the gymnasium was school, sports ground and club. Its ephēbeia enrolled young men of citizen families, about eighteen years old, for a year or two of athletic, military and civic training; finishing it was the door to citizenship. To found both in Jerusalem was to start making it a Greek city. 1 Maccabees 1:14 tells the same event without naming Jason, and adds that the young men "made foreskins for themselves" (1 Maccabees 1:15), since athletes trained naked.
orig: γυμνάσιον καὶ ἐφηβίαν (gymnasion kai ephēbian)

a: to register the Antiochenes in Jerusalem
p: Did Jason enroll all Jerusalem as citizens of Antioch, or found a Greek citizen body, "Antioch-in-Jerusalem"?
b: The Greek can mean "to register the people in Jerusalem as Antiochenes", which the KJV follows ("to write them of Jerusalem by the name of Antiochians"), or "to draw up the list of the Antiochenes in Jerusalem". Elias Bickerman argued for the second: Jason founded a Greek civic body named after the king, a "Antioch" inside Jerusalem, open to those who could pay and who joined the gymnasium. Victor Tcherikover thought Jerusalem itself became the Greek city of Antioch. Either way, citizenship would now depend on Greek education, not on the law of Moses. Venetus reads "Antiochus" for "Antiochenes".
orig: τοὺς ἐν Ἰεροσολύμοις Ἀντιοχεῖς ἀναγράψαι (tous en Hierosolymois Antiocheis anagrapsai)

a: John the father of Eupolemus
p: John won Antiochus III's charter for the Jews; his son Eupolemus later went to Rome for Judas.
b: When Antiochus III took Judea from the Ptolemies (200–198 BC), he granted the Jews the right to "live according to the laws of their own country", with gifts for the sacrifices and tax relief for the council, the priests and the temple scribes; Josephus quotes his letter (Antiquities 12.138–144). This book says those "favors" were won through John. His son Eupolemus led Judas's embassy to Rome (1 Maccabees 8:17), and he is probably the Eupolemus whose Greek history of the Jews survives in fragments. Jason's reform set aside the charter that made the law of Moses the law of the city.

a: at the very foot of the citadel
p: This citadel is the older fort beside the temple, not the Citadel the Seleucids built in 167 BC.
b: Before 167 BC Jerusalem already had a fortress (akropolis) near the temple, held by a royal garrison; Sostratus is its commander (4:28). It may be the fort north of the temple later called the Baris, though that fort is placed there only by inference from the Letter of Aristeas, and no remains have been found. Most think the Seleucid stronghold that 1 Maccabees calls "the Citadel" (hē akra, 1 Maccabees 1:33) was built later, in 167 BC; some scholars identify this akropolis with it. The gymnasium stood "right under" the fortress, near the temple, so that priests could hurry from the altar to the games (4:14). Where exactly is unknown.
orig: ὑπ᾽ αὐτὴν ἀκρόπολιν (hyp' autēn akropolin)

a: under the broad-brimmed hat
p: The petasos was the wide hat of Hermes, god of the gymnasium; wearing it marked a young man as an ephebe.
b: The petasos was a low, broad-brimmed traveler's hat, the hat of Hermes, patron of athletes, and part of the dress of the ephebes. To "bring under the petasos" is to enroll the young men in Greek training and put them under its god's sign. The Vulgate misread the phrase: Jason dared "to put all the choicest youths in brothels" (optimos quosque epheborum in lupanaribus ponere), and the Douay follows ("in brothel houses"). Nothing in the Greek speaks of brothels.
orig: ὑπὸ πέτασον ἤγαγεν (hypo petason ēgagen)

a: the Greek way
p: This is the earliest known use of Hellēnismos for a way of life, set against "Judaism" (2:21).
b: Earlier Greek writers used hellēnismos for speaking good Greek. Here, for the first time we know of, it means living as a Greek, a whole culture one can adopt. Its opposite is Ioudaismos, "Judaism", another word that appears first in this book (2:21; 8:1; 14:38), and the book adds allophylismos, "foreign ways" (also 6:24). Paul later describes his former life "in Judaism" with the same word (Galatians 1:13–14). Modern scholars borrowed "Hellenism" from this verse for the whole age after Alexander.
orig: ἀκμὴ τοῦ Ἑλληνισμοῦ καὶ πρόσβασις ἀλλοφυλισμοῦ (akmē tou Hellēnismou kai prosbasis allophylismou)

a: ungodly and no high priest
t: Was Jason a real high priest?
p: The writer denies Jason the title, though he was of the high priestly family and the king installed him.
b: Jason was Onias's brother, so by birth he could be high priest. The writer still refuses him the title because he got it by money while his brother lived, and because of what he did with it. Later Jewish writers judged other high priests by conduct as well as descent: the Dead Sea Scrolls attack a "Wicked Priest", and Josephus tells of priests who bought their office under Herod and the Romans. The book's line, holiness of life over the right family, would matter to Christian readers too (Hebrews 7:26).

a: once the discus gave its call
p: Probably the signal that opened the games, perhaps a gong; or the call to throw the discus.
b: The phrase meta tēn tou diskou prosklēsin, "after the summons of the discus", is obscure. Many think a bronze disk was struck like a gong to call the athletes to the palaestra. Others take it as the announcement of the discus event itself. Either way, the priests leave the altar of burnt offering when the gymnasium calls. The same text calls the shows paranomos chorēgia, "lawless spectacle", using the Greek word for funding public games.
orig: μετὰ τὴν τοῦ δίσκου πρόσκλησιν (meta tēn tou diskou prosklēsin)

a: the wrestling school
p: Greek athletes trained naked, which made circumcision a mark of shame for Jews who wanted to fit in.
b: The palaistra was the wrestling ground of the gymnasium. Since athletes exercised naked, a circumcised man stood out at once. 1 Maccabees 1:15 says the Hellenizers "made foreskins for themselves", probably by a surgery to stretch the skin, which ancient doctors describe. Paul knew the practice: "Was anyone called after being circumcised? Let him not undo it" (1 Corinthians 7:18, where the verb epispasthō is the medical term). The writer's point is that the priests themselves were drawn in.

a: they found enemies and avengers
p: The book's first statement of a theme it repeats: sinners are punished through the very thing they sinned by.
b: The Hellenizers wanted to be like the Greeks, and Greeks became their enemies and punishers. The pattern runs through the book: Jason, who drove many into exile, dies an exile (5:9); he who left many unburied is not buried (5:10); Andronicus is killed where he killed Onias (4:38); Antiochus, who tortured others, dies in torment (9:5–6); Menelaus dies in ashes (13:8). The rule "by what one sins, by that one is punished" is old in Israel (Psalm 7:15–16; Wisdom 11:16) and later in the Mishnah (Mishnah Sotah 1:7, "measure for measure").

a: the time that follows will make this plain
p: The writer, who is shortening a five-volume history (2:23), often stops to tell the reader what to think.
b: 2 Maccabees says it is a summary of a five-book history by Jason of Cyrene (2:23), and the summarizer speaks in his own voice. Here he promises that what follows will prove that "it is no light thing to be ungodly toward the divine laws". He will stop the story again at 5:17–20 and 6:12–17 to explain why God allowed the disasters. These asides tell first readers how to read the history: as a lesson in God's justice, not a chance series of events.

a: The games held every fifth year
p: Tyre held games every four years for its god Melqart, whom the Greeks called Heracles.
b: "Every fifth year" counts the first and the last year, as the Greeks did; in our terms it is every four years, like the Olympics. Tyre's games honored its city god Melqart, identified with Heracles. Alexander the Great had sacrificed to Heracles at Tyre and held games there after taking the city (Arrian, Anabasis 2.24; 3.6). For a delegation from Jerusalem to attend in the king's presence was a public show of loyalty to the king and his world.

a: the sacrifice to Heracles
p: Tyre's Heracles was Melqart, "king of the city", the Phoenician god some link with the Baal of Jezebel's day.
b: Herodotus visited Tyre's temple of Heracles and was told it was 2,300 years old (Herodotus 2.44). The god was Melqart, whose name means "king of the city". Some scholars think the Baal whom Jezebel of Sidon brought to Israel was Melqart (1 Kings 16:31–32), but that is debated. The writer draws no link between Melqart and Israel's God; his point is that men from Jerusalem were sent to fund a foreign god's sacrifice, and even they would not do it.

a: as Antiochenes from Jerusalem
p: The envoys go as citizens of Jason's new Greek body (4:9), a sign of the reform at work.
b: The theōroi were sacred envoys sent by one Greek city to another's festival. Jason's envoys go "as Antiochenes from Jerusalem": the new civic body of 4:9 now acts like any Greek city. The word hōs may simply mean "as"; whether the writer meant scorn, "as if", cannot be told. The detail fits Bickerman's view that "the Antiochenes in Jerusalem" were a distinct group.
orig: θεωροὺς ὡς ἀπὸ Ἰεροσολύμων Ἀντιοχέας (theōrous hōs apo Hierosolymōn Antiocheas)

a: for fitting out warships
p: Even Jason's own envoys would not pay for a pagan sacrifice. The writer lets the reform's supporters have a conscience.
b: The writer could have painted every Hellenizer as a pagan. Instead he notes that the men Jason chose balked at sacrificing to Heracles and had the money put to a civic use, the king's fleet. Historians use the detail to argue that Jason's reform was cultural and political, not yet a change of religion: Jews could join a Greek civic body and still refuse other gods. The writer's harsher view comes in 4:13–17.

a: the crowning of King Philometor
p: Ptolemy VI Philometor, Antiochus's young nephew, was proclaimed king in his own right; the date is debated.
b: Prōtoklēsia, "first proclamation", probably means the ceremony at which the young Ptolemy VI was declared of age to rule Egypt. His mother Cleopatra I was Antiochus's sister. The Egyptian court soon pressed to win back Coele-Syria, which led to the Sixth Syrian War (170–168 BC). Antiochus's visit to Joppa and Jerusalem was a tour of his southern border. Scholars date the ceremony between about 175 and 170 BC.
orig: διὰ τὰ πρωτοκλήσια τοῦ Φιλομήτορος βασιλέως (dia ta prōtoklēsia tou Philomētoros basileōs)

a: he was brought in by torchlight and with shouts
p: Greek cities greeted a visiting king with a torchlit procession and cheering, the formal 'arrival' of a ruler.
b: A king's visit was an event with fixed forms: the citizens went out to meet him, lit torches and cheered him into the city. Jerusalem under Jason gave Antiochus the full Greek welcome. Readers who knew the story would remember that within a few years the same king would enter the city as its destroyer (5:11–16).

a: Menelaus, the brother of the Simon named before
t: Menelaus: not of the high priestly line
p: Menelaus was the brother of Simon of 3:4. If they were of Benjamin, he was not even a priest.
b: Swete's Greek calls Simon "from the tribe of Benjamin" (3:4), which would make Menelaus a layman. The Old Latin reads Balgea, which many scholars take as Bilgah, a priestly family (Nehemiah 12:5, 18; 1 Chronicles 24:14). Either way, Menelaus was not of the line of high priests. The rabbis remember a Miriam of the house of Bilgah who went over to the Greeks, and they say the family was punished at the altar (Mishnah Sukkah 5:8; Tosefta Sukkah 4:28). Josephus instead makes Menelaus a brother of Onias (Antiquities 12.238–239); see the note on 4:7.

a: he flattered him with a show of authority
p: The Greek can mean Menelaus praised the king with an air of authority, or praised the king's own majestic look.
b: The words doxasas auton tō prosōpō tēs exousias are unclear. They may mean that Menelaus "glorified him with the face of authority", presenting himself as a man of standing, or that he praised the king "for the face of his power", flattering his majesty, as the KJV took it ("magnified him for the glorious appearance of his power"). The Plain chooses the first, since the sentence is about how Menelaus got the office. Either way, the office went to the higher bidder and the better courtier.
orig: δοξάσας αὐτὸν τῷ προσώπῳ τῆς ἐξουσίας (doxasas auton tō prosōpō tēs exousias)

a: the fury of a wild beast
t: The beast in the holy place
p: The writer paints Menelaus as a tyrant and a beast, the images Daniel uses for the empires.
b: The "cruel tyrant" and the "wild beast" belong to Greek invective; Greek writers called bad rulers beasts. Jewish readers would also hear Daniel, where the kingdoms of the world are beasts and Antiochus is the boastful horn of the fourth (Daniel 7:7–8; Daniel 7:23–25). Here the beast is a Jew in the high priest's robes. The book will call Antiochus "savage as a wild beast in spirit" (5:11) with a related word.

a: the land of Ammon
p: Jason fled east of the Jordan, where the Tobiad family had held a fortress and lands.
b: The "land of Ammon" is the region around modern Amman. There, Josephus says, Hyrcanus son of Joseph, of the Tobiad family, had built a stone fortress "between Arabia and Judea, beyond Jordan" and ruled the area until Antiochus IV came to the throne (Antiquities 12.230–236); its ruins at Araq el-Emir still stand. The Tobiads were rivals of the Oniads and, Josephus says, backers of Menelaus (12.239–240). Jason will come back from there with an army (5:5–7).

a: Crates, the commander of the Cyprians
p: The garrison included mercenaries from Cyprus; later the book names a 'Cypriarch' Nicanor (12:2).
b: Hellenistic kings hired soldiers from many lands and grouped them by origin. "The one over the Cypriots" was the officer of a Cypriot unit, probably part of the garrison of the citadel. 12:2 names another such officer, "Nicanor the Cypriarch". The detail shows how the writer knows the workings of the Seleucid army, and why historians value the book's information on these years even where they doubt its numbers.

a: Antiochis, the king's concubine
p: Eastern kings gave the revenues of cities to their queens and favorites; Tarsus and Mallus revolted at being given away.
b: Persian kings had assigned cities to supply a queen's clothing and jewels, a custom Greek writers mention with disapproval, and the Seleucids kept it. Tarsus (Paul's later home city, Acts 21:39) and Mallus were proud Greek cities of Cilicia, and they rose up when the king handed their revenues to his concubine. The revolt took Antiochus away from Antioch and gave Menelaus his chance.

a: Daphne, which lies near Antioch
p: Daphne was a grove and shrine of Apollo near Antioch, famous as a place of asylum.
b: Daphne, about five miles south of Antioch, had springs, a laurel grove and a great temple of Apollo; Seleucus I had made it a sanctuary where fugitives could not be touched. Antiochus IV held his famous festival there in 166 BC (Polybius 30.25–26). That Onias, the faithful high priest, took refuge in a pagan temple troubled some later readers; Josephus says nothing of it. For the writer, the scandal is that the sanctuary's oath of safety was broken (4:34).

a: At once he killed him
p: The Greek verb means 'shut out, put out of the way', a softer word for murder; the next verse calls it murder.
b: The verb parekleisen, from parakleiō, means "to shut out" and so "to put out of the way, dispatch". The KJV kept the literal "shut up", which could suggest prison. But 4:35 speaks of "the unjust murder of the man" and 4:36 of Onias "killed for no reason", so the Plain says plainly that he killed him. The oaths and the right hand make the crime worse: Andronicus broke a sworn pledge and the rule of sanctuary together.
orig: ὃν καὶ παραχρῆμα παρέκλεισεν (hon kai parachrēma parekleisen)

a: pressed him to lay hands on Onias
t: "An anointed one will be cut off"
p: Many readers, ancient and modern, find Onias's murder in Daniel 9:26 and Daniel 11:22, and in 1 Enoch 90:8.
b: Daniel, which most scholars date to the persecution of 167–164 BC, says that "After the sixty-two sevens an anointed one will be cut off, and there will be none for him" (Daniel 9:26), and that "a ruler of the covenant" will be broken (Daniel 11:22). Many scholars, and some ancient readers, take both of Onias III. The Animal Apocalypse of 1 Enoch says the ravens "seized one of those lambs" (1 Enoch 90:8), often read the same way. Christian tradition reads Daniel 9:26 of Christ, and the card on the seventy weeks at Nehemiah 2 sets out the views.

a: many people of other nations, and not Jews alone
p: The book often shows Gentiles who hate injustice: the Greeks of Antioch, the king himself, the people of Tyre.
b: 2 Maccabees is not against Greeks as such. Here "many of the other nations" are outraged at Onias's murder; Greeks join the Jews' complaint (4:36); Antiochus weeps (4:37); Tyre buries the innocent (4:49); later the people of Scythopolis are kind to Jews (12:30–31). The villains are a few greedy officials and the Jewish renegades who use them. Written for Greek-speaking Jews, the book suggests that the Jews' cause is the cause of justice, which decent Gentiles can see.

a: there he removed the murderer from the world
p: A Greek historian says Andronicus was executed for murdering the son of Seleucus IV. The two accounts may be one event.
b: Diodorus of Sicily records that "Andronicus, who assassinated the son of Seleucus" was put to death in turn (Diodorus 30.7.2). A Babylonian king list shows the boy Antiochus, son of Seleucus IV, as co-ruler until about 170 BC. Many historians think Antiochus IV had his nephew killed and then executed his agent to clear himself, and that 2 Maccabees has made Onias's murder the reason for an execution that happened for other reasons. Others think both murders were charged to Andronicus. The writer's interest is in the justice of the place: he dies where he killed.

a: So the Lord gave back to him the penalty he had earned
t: God's justice through a pagan king
p: The writer sees the Lord at work in Antiochus's anger. God uses even the persecutor to punish wrong.
b: The king acts out of grief and rage, but the writer gives the deed to the Lord, who "gave back" the fitting penalty. It is the book's first open statement that God's justice is at work in events. The same king will soon be the chief persecutor; that he can serve as God's instrument here fits the view of the prophets, who called Assyria the rod of God's anger (Isaiah 10:5). The writer's claim is a reading of providence, not something a historian can test.

a: kept robbing sacred things
p: Hierosylia, robbing a temple, was among the worst crimes in Greek law. Paul uses the same word (Romans 2:22).
b: The noun hierosylēmata means thefts from a sanctuary; Lysimachus is called "the temple robber" (hierosylos) in 4:42. Greek cities punished temple robbery with death. Paul turns the word on his readers: "You detest idols. Do you rob temples?" (Romans 2:22). The town clerk of Ephesus clears Paul's companions of the charge (Acts 19:37). For the writer, the high priest's brother is the thief, and the sacred vessels of 4:32 and 4:48 are the evidence.
orig: πολλῶν ἱεροσυλημάτων (pollōn hierosylēmatōn)

a: handfuls of the ash lying close by
p: The ash may have been from the altar of burnt offering, piled near the temple, a fitting weapon against a temple robber.
b: Some commentators think the "ash lying close by" came from the altar of burnt offering, whose ashes were carried to a place beside it (Leviticus 1:16; Leviticus 6:10–11). That would set the fight in the temple court, which fits Lysimachus's death "beside the treasury" (4:42). Others think simply of ash heaps in the street. The crowd's weapons, stones, sticks and ash, contrast with Lysimachus's three thousand armed men.

a: beside the treasury
p: The treasury held the temple funds and private deposits (3:6, 10). Jesus taught and watched gifts there.
b: The gazophylakion is the same treasury Heliodorus tried to rob (3:6–10, 24). The Gospels place Jesus there: he watched people put gifts in the treasury (Mark 12:41–44), and "He said these things in the treasury area, while teaching in the temple" (John 8:20). The temple robber dies at the place he robbed, another of the book's fitting ends.

a: three men sent by the council of elders
p: The gerousia was Jerusalem's council of elders, the body later called the Sanhedrin.
b: Antiochus III's charter had exempted "the senate" of the Jews from taxes (Josephus, Antiquities 12.142), and 2 Maccabees names the same body, the gerousia (1:10; 11:27). It sent three men to argue the case against Menelaus before the king at Tyre. Judith names the same council (Judith 4:8). It was probably the forerunner of the Sanhedrin of the New Testament (Mark 14:55).
orig: ὑπὸ τῆς γερουσίας (hypo tēs gerousias)

a: Ptolemy son of Dorymenes
p: A Seleucid general, later sent against Judas (1 Maccabees 3:38); probably the Ptolemy who pushes the persecution in 6:8.
b: 1 Maccabees 3:38 names "Ptolemy son of Dorymenes" among the generals sent against Judas in 165 BC, and 2 Maccabees 8:8 makes him governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia. He is probably the Ptolemy of 6:8, who moved the neighboring Greek cities to persecute the Jews. Here the man who takes Menelaus's bribe already has the king's ear.

a: even if they had spoken before Scythians
p: The Scythians were the Greeks' byword for savages; even they would have acquitted these men.
b: The Scythians, nomads of the steppes north of the Black Sea, were the proverbial barbarians of Greek writing (see 7:4). To say that the envoys would have been freed "even before Scythians" means that any court on earth would have found them innocent, except the king's. Paul lists "barbarian, Scythian" as the extreme of the world's divisions, which Christ overcomes (Colossians 3:11).
orig: εἰ καὶ ἐπὶ Σκυθῶν ἔλεγον (ei kai epi Skythōn elegon)

a: Wickedness grew on him
p: The verb is used of a plant or a tumor growing on something: Menelaus clung to his wickedness.
b: Epiphyomenos tē kakia means "growing upon wickedness", like a parasite plant or a growth that attaches itself. Menelaus stays in office by bribery until the end of the war, when the next king has him executed at Beroea (13:3–8), smothered in ashes, a death the writer finds fitting for one who sinned against the altar's fire and ash.
orig: ἐπιφυόμενος τῇ κακίᾳ (epiphyomenos tē kakia)

a: his second march into Egypt
t: Two Egyptian wars, one or two raids?
p: Antiochus invaded Egypt in 170/169 and 168 BC. The two books of Maccabees place the temple robbery differently.
b: Antiochus invaded Egypt in 170/169 BC and again in 168 BC, when the Roman envoy Popillius Laenas drew a circle in the sand around him and made him promise to leave before he stepped out of it (Polybius 29.27). 1 Maccabees 1:20 places the robbing of the temple in the year 143, 169 BC, after the first campaign. 2 Maccabees places it after "the second". Some historians think the king came to Jerusalem twice (Daniel 11:28–30 can be read so); others that 2 Maccabees has moved the event. Josephus gives two entries, in the years 143 and 145 (Antiquities 12.246–248).

a: horsemen running through the air
p: Ancient writers often report armies seen in the sky before a disaster. Josephus tells of the same before AD 70.
b: The vision of heavenly cavalry is a known kind of omen. Josephus says that before the Romans destroyed Jerusalem, "chariots and troops of soldiers in their armor were seen running about among the clouds" (Jewish War 6.298), and Tacitus reports armies clashing in the sky (Histories 5.13). 2 Maccabees has heavenly riders elsewhere, but as helpers (3:25; 10:29–30; 11:8). Here the meaning is unclear, so everyone prays that it means good. Elisha's servant saw "horses and fiery chariots" protecting the prophet (2 Kings 6:17).

a: the appearance meant good
p: The book's key word for God's visible help is epiphaneia, "appearance", a pun on the king's title Epiphanes.
b: Epiphaneia is the word Greeks used for a god showing himself to help his worshipers. 2 Maccabees uses it again and again for the Lord's interventions (2:21; 3:24; 12:22; 14:15; 15:27). Its use against a king who called himself Epiphanes, "(god) manifest", is pointed: the true appearances belong to the Lord. The New Testament uses the same word for Christ's coming (2 Timothy 1:10; Titus 2:13).
orig: ἐπ᾽ ἀγαθῷ τὴν ἐπιφανίαν γεγενῆσθαι (ep' agathō tēn epiphanian gegenēsthai)

a: A lying report went around that Antiochus had departed this life
p: In 168 BC a false rumor of the king's death let Jason try to take back Jerusalem by force.
b: While Antiochus was in Egypt, word spread that he was dead. Jason came back from Transjordan with a thousand men, took the city and shut Menelaus in the citadel. This civil war, not a revolt against the king, is what Antiochus treated as rebellion. Victor Tcherikover argued that the persecution answered a real uprising; this verse is part of his evidence. 1 Maccabees says nothing of Jason's coup.

a: a good day won against one's own kin is the worst day of all
t: A good day, a bad day
p: The Greek plays on euēmeria, 'a good day, success', and dysēmeria, 'a bad day, disaster'.
b: The writer's style is full of such plays on words, a mark of the polished Greek of the book. Jason thought he was "raising victory monuments" (tropaia, the trophies Greeks set up on a battlefield) over enemies. In fact he had won a civil war against his own people, the worst kind of defeat.
orig: εὐημερίαν δυσημερίαν εἶναι τὴν μεγίστην (euēmerian dysēmerian einai tēn megistēn)

a: the ruler of the Arabs
p: Aretas I is the first Nabatean ruler known by name. A later Aretas ruled Damascus in Paul's day.
b: The Nabatean Arabs, whose later capital was Petra, controlled the trade routes east and south of Judea. This Aretas is usually called Aretas I, the earliest Nabatean ruler whose name we know. The title tyrannos, "ruler", is not an insult here. 1 Maccabees 5:25 and 9:35 show the Nabateans as friends of Judas and Jonathan. Paul escaped from Damascus when "the governor under King Aretas", Aretas IV, guarded the city (2 Corinthians 11:32).

a: He had sailed to the Spartans
p: Some Jews and Spartans claimed a common ancestor in Abraham (1 Maccabees 12:21). Jason hoped to find a home there.
b: 1 Maccabees 12:5–23 gives a letter in which a Spartan king, Areus, says that Spartans and Jews are "brothers, of the family of Abraham". Most scholars doubt the letter but agree that the idea of kinship was current, and Jason, the Greek-minded high priest, counted on it. He who had made many exiles died an exile, the measure-for-measure pattern of 4:16.

a: was not mourned
p: To lie unburied and unmourned was the worst end in Israel, the fate the prophets foretold for wicked kings.
b: Jeremiah said of King Jehoiakim that no one would mourn him, "Alas, my brother", and that he would be buried with a donkey's burial, dragged off and thrown out beyond the gates (Jeremiah 22:18–19). Isaiah's taunt over the king of Babylon has him "thrown out, away from your tomb" (Isaiah 14:19). Jason, who left "crowds" of his own people unburied (5:6), gets the same end. Tobit shows how much burial mattered to the faithful (Tobit 1:17–19).

a: he judged that Judea was rebelling
p: The book says the king mistook Jason's coup for a revolt of Judea. Historians debate what set off the persecution.
b: In this book the king's fury begins with a misunderstanding: a civil war among Jews looked like rebellion. Tcherikover held that there really was a popular revolt against Menelaus and his Greek-minded supporters, which the king put down, and that the ban on the law followed. Bickerman blamed Menelaus's party for the decrees themselves. Others stress the king's humiliation in Egypt in 168 BC and his need for money and a safe border. All three can draw on this chapter.

a: Eighty thousand were destroyed in three days all told
p: Ancient writers often give round, large numbers. Josephus speaks of about ten thousand captives.
b: The figures, 80,000 lost, 40,000 killed and as many sold, are far larger than Jerusalem's population at the time is likely to have been. Josephus has the king take "about ten thousand" captives on his second entry (Antiquities 12.251). Most historians read the book's numbers as expressions of scale, not counts. The killing and the slave sales themselves are not in doubt; 1 Maccabees 1:24, 1:30–32 tells of a massacre too.

a: the temple holiest of all on earth
t: Why the king robbed the temple
p: Greek historians said Antiochus robbed the temple because he needed money. The Jewish books say pride.
b: Josephus quotes Polybius, Strabo, Nicolaus of Damascus and others as saying that Antiochus "broke his league with the Jews" and plundered their temple because he was short of money (Against Apion 2.84). Polybius also says he robbed most temples in his kingdom (Polybius 30.26). 2 Maccabees adds a theological reason: the king's pride (5:17, 21) and the people's sins (5:17–18). 1 Maccabees 1:21–23 lists what he took: the gold altar, the lampstand, the table and the cups.

a: The gifts many kings had set up
p: Persian and Greek kings had given gifts to the Jerusalem temple; 3:2–3 says Seleucus IV paid for its sacrifices.
b: The temple held many gifts from foreign rulers. Persian kings paid for sacrifices and vessels (Ezra 6:8–10; Ezra 7:15–20), Antiochus III gave money for sacrifices and repairs (Josephus, Antiquities 12.140–141), and 2 Maccabees says that even Seleucus IV met the costs of the sacrifices from his revenues (3:3). Antiochus IV reverses his fathers' policy. The "foul" and "unholy" hands that sweep them up are the opposite of the clean hands the temple demands (Psalm 24:3–4).

a: the Master had grown angry for a short while
p: The writer explains the disaster as God's brief anger at his people's sins, as the prophets did after the exile.
b: God's anger with his people is short, his mercy long: "For a little moment I abandoned you, / but with great tenderness I will gather you in" (Isaiah 54:7). The writer applies the prophets' reading of the Babylonian disaster to the crisis of his own time. The phrase returns in the mouth of the youngest brother: the Lord is angry "for a short time" and will be reconciled (7:33). The word "Master" (despotēs) is one of the book's names for God.

a: as happened to Heliodorus
t: Why Heliodorus failed and Antiochus did not
p: The book answers the obvious question: why did God protect the temple in chapter 3 but not now?
b: In chapter 3 heavenly riders flogged Heliodorus when he tried to enter the treasury (3:24–30). Why did nothing stop Antiochus? Because, the writer says, Onias's people then were faithful (3:1), and now they were "tangled in many sins". The temple is safe only as long as the people keep the covenant. The prophets had said the same of the first temple (Jeremiah 7:4–14).

a: he chose the place for the sake of the nation
p: God chose the temple for the people, not the people for the temple. The saying recalls Jeremiah and later Jesus.
b: The sentence answers anyone who thought the temple guaranteed safety. Jeremiah had warned against trusting in "The LORD's temple, the LORD's temple, the LORD's temple" while doing wrong (Jeremiah 7:4). The shape of the saying is like Jesus' "The Sabbath came into being for the sake of human beings, and not human beings for the sake of the Sabbath" (Mark 2:27). In John, the priests fear the Romans will "take from us our place and our nation alike" (John 11:48), putting the two words side by side as here.

a: when the great Master made peace
p: 2 Maccabees speaks of God being reconciled to his people; Paul speaks of God reconciling people to himself.
b: The noun is katallagē, "reconciliation". In 2 Maccabees it is God who becomes reconciled, his anger ended by the people's prayer, repentance and the martyrs' deaths (1:5; 7:33; 8:29). Paul uses the same word family but turns it around: "God was reconciling the world to himself in Christ" (2 Corinthians 5:19), and "we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son" (Romans 5:10). The change in who is reconciled to whom is one of the clearest differences between the two.
orig: ἐν τῇ τοῦ μεγάλου δεσπότου καταλλαγῇ (en tē tou megalou despotou katallagē)

a: make dry land fit for ships and the open sea fit to march across
p: Greek readers knew this boast: Xerxes cut a canal for ships through a peninsula and bridged the sea for his army.
b: The Persian king Xerxes dug a canal across the Athos peninsula and bridged the Hellespont so his army could march over the sea (Herodotus 7.22–24; 7.33–36). Greek writers made him the model of pride that challenges the order of nature, and so the gods. Antiochus is painted in the same colors. Jewish readers would hear the king of Babylon's boast, "I will go up into the heavens" (Isaiah 14:13). The book will make the point again when Antiochus, who thought he could command the waves, is carried in a litter (9:8).

a: Philip, a Phrygian by birth
p: Philip governed Jerusalem for the king; he burns the Sabbath-keepers in the caves (6:11).
b: Philip, from Phrygia in Asia Minor, was the king's man in Jerusalem. He burns those keeping the Sabbath in caves (6:11) and calls for help when Judas wins (8:8). He is probably not the Philip whom Antiochus later made regent for his son (9:29; 1 Maccabees 6:14). "More savage than the one who placed him there" means even worse than the king.

a: at Gerizim, Andronicus
p: The king set a governor over the Samaritans' temple on Mount Gerizim as well (6:2).
b: The Samaritans had their own temple on Mount Gerizim above Shechem (John 4:20). The king's governor there was another Andronicus, not the one executed in 4:38. The book treats the Samaritans as part of "the race" that suffered, and their temple too was renamed (6:2). Josephus tells it differently: the Samaritans asked the king to rename their temple (Antiquities 12.257–264).

a: Apollonius, the commander of the Mysians
p: Mysarchēs most likely means commander of Mysian troops; the KJV took it as 'detestable ringleader'.
b: The Greek title mysarchēs most likely means "leader of the Mysians", soldiers from Mysia in Asia Minor, a known group in the Seleucid army. The KJV heard mysos, "abomination", and wrote "that detestable ringleader", a pun the writer may have enjoyed. 1 Maccabees 1:29 tells of the same attack by "an officer to collect tribute"; many scholars think a Hebrew title was confused in one book or the other (see the note there). He may be the Apollonius governor of Samaria whom Judas killed (1 Maccabees 3:10–12).
orig: τὸν μυσάρχην Ἀπολλώνιον (ton mysarchēn Apollōnion)

a: He held off until the holy day of the Sabbath
p: The enemy knew the Jews would not fight on the Sabbath. 1 Maccabees tells a similar Sabbath massacre.
b: An enemy who waited for the Sabbath could attack without resistance. 1 Maccabees 2:29–38 tells how a thousand people in the wilderness let themselves be killed rather than break the Sabbath, after which Mattathias decided to fight back if attacked on that day (1 Maccabees 2:41). 2 Maccabees, which has no Mattathias, shows Judas resting on the Sabbath after victory (8:26–28) and Nicanor planning to attack on it (15:1–5). See also 6:11.

a: Judas, also called Maccabeus
p: 2 Maccabees brings in Judas here without his father Mattathias. Hebrews 11:38 may remember such scenes.
b: In 1 Maccabees the revolt begins with the priest Mattathias at Modein and his flight to the hills with his sons (1 Maccabees 2:1–28). 2 Maccabees never names Mattathias; Judas appears suddenly here, "one of about ten", living like wild animals and eating plants rather than unclean food. Hebrews 11:38 describes faithful people "wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and holes in the ground", which many readers link with these years. Daniel ate vegetables rather than the king's food (Daniel 1:12).

a: an elderly Athenian
t: An old man, a senator, or Geron?
p: Gerōn can mean 'old man', 'elder (council member)', or be a name, Geron. The Latin made him a man of Antioch.
b: The phrase geronta Athēnaion is usually read "an old Athenian" (KJV "an old man of Athens"). Some take gerōn as a member of a council, "an Athenian senator"; others as a name, "Geron the Athenian". Why an Athenian? Perhaps because Athens was the center of Greek religion, or because he was an expert in cults. The Vulgate makes him "a certain old man of Antioch" (see the variant).
orig: γέροντα Ἀθηναῖον (geronta Athēnaion)

a: so that they no longer governed their lives by the laws of God
p: The decree undid Antiochus III's charter that let the Jews live by their ancestral laws.
b: The words answer Antiochus III's grant of 200 BC, that the Jews might "live according to the laws of their own country" (Josephus, Antiquities 12.142). The verb politeuesthai, "live as citizens, govern one's life", belongs to Greek constitutional language. 1 Maccabees 1:41–50 describes the same decree in more detail: an end to sacrifice, Sabbath, feasts and circumcision, and the building of pagan altars. In 167 BC Judaism became, for a time, illegal in its own land.

a: name it for Olympian Zeus
p: The temple was renamed for Zeus Olympios. Many think the god was the Syrian 'Lord of Heaven' under a Greek name.
b: Antiochus favored Olympian Zeus; he paid for work on the great Olympieion in Athens (Polybius 26.1). Renaming the Jerusalem temple put Israel's God under the name of the head of the Greek gods. Many scholars think the local population would have understood "Zeus" as Baal Shamem, "Lord of Heaven", and that Daniel's "abomination of desolation" (shiqquts shomem) mocks that name (Daniel 11:31; Daniel 12:11). 1 Maccabees 1:54 tells of the abomination built on the altar; see the note there.

a: Zeus, Protector of Guests, as befitted those who dwelt there
p: Gerizim's temple became Zeus Xenios's. Josephus says the Samaritans asked for the name 'Zeus Hellenios'.
b: Zeus Xenios was the god who protects guests and strangers. "As befitted those who dwelt there" may mean that the Samaritans were known as hospitable, or that they were themselves foreigners in Jewish eyes (2 Kings 17:24–41). Josephus quotes a letter in which "the Sidonians who live at Shechem" ask the king to name their nameless temple "the Temple of Jupiter Hellenius" (Zeus of the Greeks), and the king agrees (Antiquities 12.257–264). Many historians doubt the letter, which serves Josephus's low view of the Samaritans.

a: The temple was filled with wild living and drunken revels by the Gentiles
p: Greek festivals included banquets and drink; for Jews the presence of Gentiles in the courts was itself defilement.
b: Greek temple worship included feasting on the sacrifices, wine and, in some cults, sacred prostitution, though how far this happened in Jerusalem is not known. The writer piles up words of disorder: debauchery, revels, prostitutes, women in the holy precincts, "things that did not belong there". The law kept women out of the inner courts during their periods and barred Gentiles from the temple proper; later a stone warning in Greek threatened death to any foreigner who went past the barrier.

a: or simply to say, "I am a Jew."
p: Confessing one's identity became a crime. The words prefigure the Christian martyrs' answer, "I am a Christian."
b: The verb is homologein, "to confess, acknowledge". The persecution made a simple statement of who one was a capital offense. Two centuries later Christian martyrs gave the same kind of answer before Roman judges; Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, told the proconsul, "I am a Christian" (Martyrdom of Polycarp 10.1). Jesus had said, "everyone who openly declares for me in front of people" (Matthew 10:32), with the same verb. On how Christian martyr stories drew on 2 Maccabees, see the chapter page.
orig: ἁπλῶς Ἰουδαῖον ὁμολογεῖν εἶναι (haplōs Ioudaion homologein einai)

a: on the king's birthday
p: Hellenistic kings kept a monthly feast on the day of their birth, with sacrifices in their honor.
b: Inscriptions show that some Hellenistic kings had their birthday celebrated every month, on the same day of the month, with sacrifices and feasts. Jews were "led off under bitter compulsion" to eat the sacrificial meat, the splanchna, the inner organs roasted and eaten first at a Greek sacrifice. Taking part meant sharing in worship of the king and his gods. The same word, splanchnismos, runs through the martyr stories (6:8, 21; 7:42).
orig: εἰς τὴν κατὰ μῆνα τοῦ βασιλέως γενέθλιον ἡμέραν ἐπὶ σπλαγχνισμόν (eis tēn kata mēna tou basileōs genethlion hēmeran epi splanchnismon)

a: they were made to march in Dionysus's parade carrying ivy
p: Ivy was the plant of Dionysus, god of wine. 3 Maccabees tells of Jews branded with his ivy leaf.
b: Dionysus's worshipers wore ivy wreaths and carried the thyrsus, a staff topped with ivy (compare Judith 15:12). The Seleucid and Ptolemaic kings promoted his cult. 3 Maccabees, a Greek Jewish story set in Egypt, has Ptolemy IV order Jews to be branded with "the ivy leaf of Dionysus" (3 Maccabees 2:29). Being forced to march in his procession was a public act of worship of another god.

a: At Ptolemy's suggestion
p: The persecution spread to the Greek cities near Judea, either at Ptolemy's urging or at the request of Ptolemais.
b: The decree extended the persecution to Jews living in the Greek cities around Judea. Swete's text credits it to Ptolemy, probably the governor of 4:45 and 8:8. The Latin reads "the Ptolemaeans", the people of Ptolemais (Acco), who were hostile to the Jews (1 Maccabees 5:15; 1 Maccabees 12:48), and some editors correct the Greek to match. See the variant.
orig: Πτολεμαίου ὑποθεμένου (Ptolemaiou hypothemenou)

a: Two women were brought up for having circumcised their children
p: 1 Maccabees and Josephus tell the same cruelty: mothers killed with the babies they had circumcised.
b: "They put to death the women who had had their children circumcised", and hung the babies from their necks (1 Maccabees 1:60–61). Josephus also tells that circumcised infants and their mothers were put to death (Antiquities 12.256). Circumcision on the eighth day was the sign of the covenant (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3). By keeping it, these mothers chose the covenant over their own lives and their children's.

a: to keep the seventh day in secret
p: Those who would not defend themselves on the Sabbath were burned in their caves. 1 Maccabees 2 tells a similar story.
b: 1 Maccabees 2:29–38 tells of a thousand men, women and children in the wilderness who would not fight on the Sabbath and were killed. Mattathias then decided that Jews may defend themselves if attacked on the Sabbath (1 Maccabees 2:39–41). This verse reflects the stricter view that held back "in fear of God". The rabbis later taught that saving life overrides the Sabbath (Talmud, Yoma 85a–b). Jesus asked whether it is lawful "to save life or to kill" on the Sabbath (Mark 3:4).

a: So I appeal to anyone who picks up this book
t: The writer speaks to his readers
p: The writer interrupts the story to tell his readers how to understand the suffering before he tells the worst of it.
b: The summarizer, who says he has shortened Jason of Cyrene's five volumes (2:23), addresses "those who come upon this book". The pause comes just before the martyr stories, so that his readers will not lose heart at what follows. He ends his book the same way (15:37–39). Ancient historians did write such comments, but this one is a sermon: suffering is God's discipline.

a: but for the correction of our people
t: Compared with the Bible: suffering as discipline
p: The teaching agrees with Deuteronomy, Proverbs and Hebrews: God disciplines his children because he loves them.
b: Agrees. "The LORD your God trains you the way a man trains his son" (Deuteronomy 8:5); "For whoever the LORD loves, he rebukes" (Proverbs 3:12), a verse Hebrews quotes to say that suffering proves we are God's children (Hebrews 12:5–11). Goes beyond. 2 Maccabees adds a contrast: God punishes Israel quickly so its sins do not pile up, while he lets the nations' sins reach their full measure (6:14–15). Wisdom of Solomon says much the same (Wisdom 12:22). Job warns against applying the rule too quickly to a sufferer; on whether suffering is God's discipline, the churches' answers are on the card at Job 5.

a: until they have come to the point where their sins are full
p: The idea that judgment waits until a people's sins are full goes back to Genesis 15:16.
b: God told Abraham that his descendants would wait for the land because "the guilt of the Amorites is not yet full" (Genesis 15:16). Daniel 8:23 speaks of a time "when the rebels have reached their full measure", and Jesus says, "You, then, fill up your fathers' measure!" (Matthew 23:32). Paul uses the image of those who hinder the gospel (1 Thessalonians 2:16). The writer turns it into comfort: Israel is punished early so that it is never punished to the end.

a: He trains his own people by misfortune, yet he never leaves them
p: The promise that God disciplines but does not abandon his people echoes the Law and the Psalms.
b: The covenant curses end with a promise: "even while they are in the land of their enemies, I will not reject them" (Leviticus 26:44). The psalmist says, "For the LORD will not let go of his people" (Psalm 94:14). The fifth brother says the same to the king: "do not imagine that our race has been deserted by God" (7:16). Paul asks, "Has God rejected his people?" and answers no (Romans 11:1).

a: Eleazar, one of the foremost scribes
p: Eleazar is an elderly teacher of the law. 4 Maccabees makes him a priest; churches honor him on 1 August.
b: A "scribe" here is a teacher and interpreter of the law, as Ezra was (Ezra 7:6). 4 Maccabees retells his death at length and calls him a priest, "of priestly family" and expert in the law (4 Maccabees 5:4). He is not the Eleazar killed by the elephant in 1 Maccabees 6:43–46. With the mother and her seven sons, he is remembered by the Orthodox churches on 1 August as one of the Holy Maccabees, and the Roman Martyrology keeps the same day.

a: pig's meat
p: Pork was the test because the law named the pig as unclean, and Greeks offered pigs in sacrifice.
b: "The pig has a split hoof, divided all the way through, but it does not chew the cud. It is unclean for you" (Leviticus 11:7; compare Deuteronomy 14:8). Isaiah condemned those "who eat the meat of pigs" in pagan rites (Isaiah 65:4). Pigs were common sacrifices in Greek cults, and 1 Maccabees 1:47 says the king ordered swine offered. Eating pork was therefore both breaking the law and joining the king's worship. On the food laws for Christians, see the card at Leviticus 11.

a: the torture frame
p: Eleazar is beaten on a tympanon. Hebrews 11:35 uses its verb for those who were 'tortured, not accepting release'.
b: A tympanon is literally a drum. Here it is a frame or wheel on which a victim was stretched and beaten to death (6:30, "under the blows"). Hebrews 11:35 uses the verb made from it, etympanisthēsan: "others were tortured, not accepting release, so that they might gain a better resurrection". The rare verb, the refused release (6:21–22, 30; 7:24) and the hope of resurrection (7:9–14) make most commentators think Hebrews is remembering these martyrs.
orig: ἐπὶ τὸ τύμπανον (epi to tympanon)

a: spitting it out first
p: The Greek of 6:19–20 is hard to construe; the Plain follows the most common reading.
b: "Spitting out first" (proptysas) most likely means he spat out the meat forced into his mouth (6:18). The rest of the sentence holds him up as the model for "those who stand firm to fight off what is forbidden to taste". Alexandrinus lacks the words "for (the love of)", and Venetus's corrector wrote a different verb. The Latin smooths it into "considering how he ought to come". The KJV divides the verses differently and puts "spit it forth" in 6:19.
orig: προπτύσας δέ, καθ᾽ ὃν ἔδει τρόπον προσέρχεσθαι (proptysas de, kath' hon edei tropon proserchesthai)

a: to act as though he were eating
p: Eleazar refuses even to seem to eat, because the young would be misled. The question of pretense runs through church history.
b: His friends offered a way out: bring permitted meat and pretend it was the sacrifice. Eleazar's reason for refusing is not only his own purity but the effect on others (6:24–25). Paul argued the same way: "if food trips up my brother, I will never eat meat again" (1 Corinthians 8:13; compare Romans 14:15). In the persecutions of the early church, Christians who bought certificates of sacrifice without sacrificing were treated as lapsed (Cyprian, On the Lapsed), and in the Reformation Calvin wrote against Protestants who hid their faith by outward conformity.

a: telling them to send him on to Hades
p: Hades is the Greek name for the world of the dead, the Septuagint's word for Sheol.
b: The Septuagint uses Hadēs for Hebrew Sheol, the world of the dead (Psalm 16:10; Acts 2:27). "Send me on to Hades" means "kill me now". It does not say what Eleazar expected after death, but 6:26 shows he believed God's judgment reached "alive or dead", and the brothers in chapter 7 hope for resurrection. Jesus speaks of Hades as a place where the dead are aware (Luke 16:23).
orig: προπέμπειν εἰς τὸν ᾅδην (propempein eis ton hadēn)

a: Eleazar, ninety years old
p: Eleazar fears the young will think he has gone over to allophylismos, the same 'foreign ways' as 4:13.
b: The word allophylismos, "the ways of other tribes", is the one the writer used for Jason's reform (4:13). Eleazar sees what is at stake: not one meal, but whether the people's teachers will lead the young into the Greek way. His age, ninety, adds weight; Abraham laughed at a son for "a woman of ninety" (Genesis 17:17), and the law commands honor for the old (Leviticus 19:32).
orig: Ἐλεάζαρον τὸν ἐνενηκονταετῆ μεταβεβηκέναι εἰς ἀλλοφυλισμόν (Eleazaron ton enenēkontaetē metabebēkenai eis allophylismon)

a: I will not slip out of the hands of the Almighty, alive or dead
p: Eleazar fears God more than the king, because God's judgment reaches beyond death.
b: The idea that God's hand reaches the dead goes with the hope of resurrection in chapter 7. Jesus put it plainly: "do not fear the people who kill the body but have no power to kill the soul. Instead, fear the One who can destroy soul and body alike in Gehenna" (Matthew 10:28). The psalmist knew no place could hide him from God, even Sheol (Psalm 139:8).

a: to meet a good death
p: The Greek verb is related to 'euthanasia', but it means to die nobly, not mercy killing.
b: Apeuthanatizein means "to die well", to meet death with honor. Its root is the same as the modern word "euthanasia", which first meant an easy or happy death and only in modern times came to mean ending a life to spare suffering. Eleazar's "good death" is the opposite of escape: he chooses pain rather than a pretense that would have saved him. 1 Maccabees has Judas say it is better "to die fighting" than see the nation's ruin (1 Maccabees 3:59).
orig: ἀπευθανατίζειν (apeuthanatizein)

a: but in my soul I suffer this with joy, because of my fear of him
p: Body in pain, soul glad: the martyr's paradox, which the New Testament also teaches.
b: The contrast of body and soul is Greek in form, but the reason is Jewish: "because of my fear of him". 4 Maccabees builds a whole book on it, arguing that devout reason rules the passions. The apostles left the council "glad at heart, because they had been found worthy to be dishonored for the sake of the Name" (Acts 5:41), and Jesus told his followers to "be glad and celebrate" when persecuted (Matthew 5:11–12).

a: He left his death behind as a pattern of nobility
p: Eleazar's death is a hypodeigma, a pattern to copy. James uses the same word for the prophets' suffering.
b: The word hypodeigma, "example, pattern", sums up why the story is told: so that others will do the same (6:28). James writes, "take as an example (hypodeigma) of suffering and patience the prophets" (James 5:10). Hebrews 11 lists heroes of faith in the same spirit, and many think Hebrews 11:35 includes Eleazar. Christian preachers from the fourth century held him up as a model for the clergy and the old (Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 15).
orig: ὑπόδιγμα γενναιότητος καὶ μνημόσυνον ἀρετῆς (hypodigma gennaiotētos kai mnēmosynon aretēs)

a: seven brothers were arrested along with their mother
p: The book does not name them or the place. Later Jews and Christians gave the mother names and placed the story in Antioch.
b: 2 Maccabees gives no names and no place; the king's presence suggests Antioch, or Jerusalem if the king had come there. 4 Maccabees retells the story at length. Christians in Antioch honored a shrine of the Maccabean martyrs by the late fourth century (Augustine, Sermon 300, mentions their church there), and Orthodox tradition calls the mother Solomonia. In Jewish tradition she is unnamed in the Talmud, Miriam bat Nahtom ("daughter of Nahtom", a name that means "baker") in Lamentations Rabbah, and Hannah in the longer version of the medieval Josippon, the name most later tradition uses. Many historians think the story is a model tale of martyrdom built on real events of 167 BC; others see no reason to doubt that such deaths happened.

a: the laws of our fathers
p: Patrioi nomoi, 'ancestral laws', was the phrase of royal charters. The martyrs die for what the king had once granted.
b: The phrase patrioi nomoi was the legal term for a people's inherited customs, the very thing Antiochus III had allowed the Jews to keep (see the note on 6:1). The brothers die "for the laws of our fathers" (7:2, 37) and for "his laws", God's (7:9, 11, 23). In this book the law is not a set of rules alone but the covenant life of a people, given "through Moses" (7:30).
orig: πατρῴους νόμους παραβαίνειν (patrōous nomous parabainein)

a: strip off his scalp the way the Scythians do
p: Herodotus describes how Scythian warriors took their enemies' scalps.
b: The verb periskythizein, "to Scythianize all around", means to cut away the scalp. Herodotus describes how Scythian warriors scalped the men they killed and hung the scalps from their bridles (Herodotus 4.64). The tortures of this chapter, tongue, scalp, hands and feet, frying, are told with care so that the reader feels the cost of faithfulness. See also 4:47.
orig: περισκυθίσαντας ἀκρωτηριάζειν (periskythisantas akrōtēriazein)

a: 'And he will show his servants pity.'
p: The brothers quote Deuteronomy 32:36, from the song Moses gave as a witness. 4 Maccabees has the mother teach the same song.
b: The quotation follows the Greek of Deuteronomy 32:36, kai epi tois doulois autou paraklēthēsetai, "and he will be comforted (have compassion) over his servants"; the site's Plain from the Hebrew reads "and show his servants pity". Moses said that "this song will testify against them as a witness" (Deuteronomy 31:21): it foretold Israel's sin, its punishment, and God's turning back to it. That is the book's whole reading of the persecution. 4 Maccabees 18:18–19 has the mother remember the father teaching the song, "I kill, and I make alive" (Deuteronomy 32:39).
orig: Καὶ ἐπὶ τοῖς δούλοις αὐτοῦ παρακληθήσεται (Kai epi tois doulois autou paraklēthēsetai)

a: for their cruel game
p: The word empaigmos, 'mockery', is the one Hebrews 11:36 uses: 'others had a trial of mockings and floggings.'
b: The noun empaigmos means mocking or cruel sport. It is rare in Greek, and Hebrews 11:36 uses it right after the tortured of 11:35: "Others had a trial of mockings and floggings, and even chains and prison." With the "floggings" (mastiges, 7:1) and the torture frame (6:19), it is part of the evidence that Hebrews has these martyrs in mind. The Gospels use the related verb of the soldiers who mocked Jesus (Mark 15:20).
orig: ἐπὶ τὸν ἐμπαιγμόν (epi ton empaigmon)

a: He replied in his fathers' tongue
p: Probably Hebrew or Aramaic. The brothers speak to each other in a language the king does not understand.
b: "The ancestral voice" (tē patriō phōnē) is probably Hebrew, which the book elsewhere uses for battle cries and hymns (12:37; 15:29), though some think of Aramaic. The detail recurs (7:21, 27): the mother can encourage her sons while the king thinks she is persuading them. Language marks the line between the two peoples, as Jason's reform tried to erase it.
orig: τῇ πατρίῳ φωνῇ (tē patriō phōnē)

a: You fiend
p: An alastōr was an avenging spirit or an accursed man, one who brings guilt and ruin on himself.
b: In Greek tragedy an alastōr is a spirit of vengeance that pursues a crime, or a man so wicked he is a curse. The KJV has "Thou like a fury". The second brother does not plead; he names the king as one under a curse, and then states the hope that makes the curse powerless.
orig: Σὺ μέν, ἀλάστωρ (Sy men, alastōr)

a: But the King of the world will raise us, who died for his laws, to live again forever
t: Compared with the Bible: the resurrection
p: This is one of the clearest statements of bodily resurrection before the New Testament.
b: Agrees with Daniel, "Many of those asleep in the dusty ground will wake up. Some will wake to life without end" (Daniel 12:2), and Isaiah 26:19. Goes beyond most of the Hebrew Bible, where the dead go to Sheol and the hope of rising is rare. The New Testament shares this hope: Martha says, "I know he will rise... at the resurrection on the last day" (John 11:24), and Jesus is "the resurrection and the life" (John 11:25). The Catholic Catechism cites this verse and 7:14 for the growth of the hope (Catechism 992). Protestants who do not count the book as Scripture still read it as evidence of what Jews believed before Jesus.

a: from him I hope to receive them back
t: Compared with the Bible: the same body
p: The third brother expects to get back the very tongue and hands he loses, the strongest picture of bodily resurrection here.
b: Agrees. The resurrection is of the body: Jesus showed his hands and side (John 20:20, 27). Goes beyond, or differs. Paul says the body is sown "natural" and raised "spiritual", changed as a seed is changed into a plant (1 Corinthians 15:35–44), which some read as more than getting back the same limbs. Catholic teaching says all will rise "with their own bodies which they now bear" (Fourth Lateran Council, quoted in the Catechism 999). Razis's death, tearing out his entrails and asking the Lord to give them back (14:46), carries the same hope to its limit.

a: For you, though, there will be no resurrection to life
p: The brother denies the king a 'resurrection to life'. Is there no rising at all for the wicked, or a rising to judgment?
b: 2 Maccabees speaks of resurrection only for the faithful. Some read this verse as saying the wicked will not rise at all. Others note the words "to life": the king may rise, but not to life. Daniel 12:2 has some rise "to everlasting life" and some "to disgrace", and Jesus says, "Those who did good will go out to a resurrection that brings life. Those who did wicked things will go out to a resurrection that brings judgment" (John 5:29). Two questions follow. Will the wicked rise? Most Christian traditions, Adventists among them, say yes, to judgment; Jehovah's Witnesses teach that those judged wholly wicked are not raised. Is their punishment endless? Most say yes; Adventists teach that after the judgment the wicked are destroyed.

a: how he will torment you and your offspring
p: The fifth brother's warning comes true in chapter 9: Antiochus dies in agony, and his son is killed young.
b: Antiochus is struck with pain in his bowels and dies in torment far from home (9:5–28), and his son Antiochus V is killed by Demetrius's men in 162 BC (14:2; 1 Maccabees 7:2–4). The writer's readers knew both events, so the brothers' words read as prophecy. The same pattern, persecutor punished, closes Daniel's vision of the king of the north (Daniel 11:45).

a: We suffer this because of ourselves; we sinned against our own God
t: Suffering for sins, or for God?
p: The martyrs say they suffer for the nation's sins, though they themselves are innocent. Two ideas meet here.
b: The sixth brother, like the seventh (7:32), says "we suffer for our own sins". He speaks for the nation: the persecution is God's discipline of Israel (6:12–16). Yet the brothers die because they will not sin. The book holds both ideas: the people's sins brought the disaster, and the innocent who die faithful help end it (7:37–38). Psalm 44 had already complained that Israel suffered though it had not forgotten God: "it is on your account that we are killed all day long" (Psalm 44:22).

a: after you have set out to fight against God
p: The Greek theomachein, 'to fight God', returns in the Gamaliel speech of Acts 5:39.
b: The verb theomachein was used in Greek tragedy of mortals who defied the gods, such as Pentheus against Dionysus. The sixth brother applies it to the king. Gamaliel warns the council against the apostles: "You might even turn out to be fighting against God" (Acts 5:39), where the Greek is theomachoi, "God-fighters". Antiochus's own words on his deathbed will admit it (9:12).
orig: θεομαχεῖν ἐπιχειρήσας (theomachein epicheirēsas)

a: she is worth remembering for good
t: The feast of the Holy Maccabees
p: Christians honored the mother, her sons and Eleazar as martyrs from the 300s on. Their feast is 1 August.
b: By the late fourth century Christians kept a feast of the Maccabean martyrs. Gregory of Nazianzus preached on it, saying few honored them "because their martyrdom antedates Christ" (Oration 15); John Chrysostom preached homilies on them; Augustine, in North Africa, called them martyrs of Christ (Sermon 300). The Orthodox churches keep the Holy Maccabees on 1 August, at the start of the Dormition fast, and the Roman Martyrology keeps the same day; until 1969 it was also a feast of the General Roman Calendar. They are among the very few pre-Christian figures honored in the church's calendar of martyrs.

a: she stirred her womanly thinking with a manly heart
t: A woman with a man's courage
p: The ancient phrase assumes courage is 'manly'. 4 Maccabees goes further, calling her stronger than men.
b: Greek writers praised brave women as "manly" (arsēn thymos, "male spirit"); the phrase reflects its time. The writer's real point is that she outdid everyone: "good beyond all measure" (7:20). 4 Maccabees calls her "mother of the nation, defender of the law" and says she "stood firmer than men" (4 Maccabees 15:29–30; 16:14).
orig: τὸν θῆλυν λογισμὸν ἄρσενι θυμῷ διεγείρασα (ton thēlyn logismon arseni thymō diegeirasa)

a: How you showed up in my womb, I cannot say
p: The mother echoes the Psalms and Job: God, not the mother, forms a child in the womb.
b: The psalmist says to God, "you wove me together in my mother's womb" (Psalm 139:13), and Job, "With skin and flesh you clothed me; / with bones and sinews you wove me together" (Job 10:11). Ecclesiastes says no one knows how the bones grow in a pregnant woman's womb (Ecclesiastes 11:5). The breath of life comes from God, as in Genesis, when he "blew into his nostrils the breath of life" (Genesis 2:7). Her argument follows: the God who gave life the first time can give it again (7:23).

a: the Creator of the world
t: Creator and giver of life again
p: The mother argues from creation to resurrection: the one who made life can restore it.
b: Ho tou kosmou ktistēs, "the Creator of the world", is a title found in Greek Jewish writings (1:24; 4 Maccabees 5:25) and in 1 Peter 4:19, "a faithful Creator". The argument from creation to resurrection is the heart of the chapter: as God gave "breath and life" in the womb, so he will give them back. Paul argues the same way: God "makes the dead alive and calls the things that are not as though they were" (Romans 4:17).
orig: ὁ τοῦ κόσμου κτίστης (ho tou kosmou ktistēs)

a: he would have him as a Friend
p: 'Friend' was a court rank. The king offers the last son a career at court if he will give up the law.
b: "Friend" (philos) was a title of the Seleucid court, as in 1 Maccabees (1 Maccabees 2:18; 1 Maccabees 10:65). Joining the Friends meant wealth, honor and "important tasks", royal offices. The offer echoes the one made to Mattathias in 1 Maccabees 2:18. The same choice, career or faith, faced Jews who joined Jason's gymnasium.
orig: φίλον ἕξειν καὶ χρείας ἐμπιστεύσειν (philon hexein kai chreias empisteusein)

a: laughing at the savage tyrant
p: The king asks the mother to persuade her son. She agrees, then speaks in Hebrew and urges him to die.
b: The king takes her promise at face value; she "laughs at" him and speaks in the ancestral tongue, which he cannot follow. Some readers have been troubled that she seems to deceive the king. Others note that she promised to "win her son over" (7:26) and does, to the side of God. Her mockery of a tyrant who cannot understand her is like Judith's double-edged words to Holofernes (Judith 11:5–19).

a: I nursed you three years
p: Children were weaned late in the ancient world, often at about three years old.
b: Weaning at about three was common in Israel and its neighbors. Hannah kept Samuel until he was weaned (1 Samuel 1:22–24), and a feast marked Isaac's weaning (Genesis 21:8). The mother's list, nine months in the womb, three years at the breast, years of rearing, sets her love against the king's offer.

a: Know that God made them, not from things that were
p: Origen and the Catechism read ouk ex ontōn as creation from nothing; many modern scholars think it says less.
b: The Greek is ouk ex ontōn epoiēsen auta ho theos, "God made them not out of existing things". The Vulgate made it plain, ex nihilo, "from nothing", and Christian theology has read it so since Origen, who cites "the mother of the seven martyrs" for creation from nothing (Origen, On First Principles 2.1.5). The Catholic Catechism quotes the verse for creation "out of nothing" (Catechism 297). Many modern scholars doubt that it already teaches the later, strict doctrine, which denies that any matter existed before God made the world. Gerhard May finds in it no more than the idea that the world came into being by God's sovereign act, and says that rejecting eternal matter lies outside the text's horizon; Xenophon used "to bring forth from what is not" in an everyday sense (Memorabilia 2.2.3). Jonathan Goldstein (1984) also denied that the verse teaches creation from nothing. His wider claim, that the doctrine arose to defend bodily resurrection, was answered by David Winston (1986), and Goldstein partly withdrew it (1987). Paul Copan, against May, defends the older reading. The Plain keeps the Greek's wording.
orig: ὅτι οὐκ ἐξ ὄντων ἐποίησεν αὐτὰ ὁ θεός (hoti ouk ex ontōn epoiēsen auta ho theos)

a: and the human race comes to be in the same way
t: Compared with the Bible: creation from nothing
p: The verse is a key text for creation out of nothing. Compare Genesis 1, Hebrews 11:3 and Romans 4:17.
b: Agrees with the direction of the 66 books, where God alone makes all things (Nehemiah 9:6; John 1:3) and "what is seen" did not come from "things that appear" (Hebrews 11:3). Goes beyond Genesis 1:1–2, which does not say what was before "The earth was shapeless and empty". Wisdom of Solomon, another Greek Jewish book, says God made the world "out of formless matter" (Wisdom 11:17), so the two books may not mean the same thing. The mother's point is practical: the God who made the world, and makes each child, from nothing can raise her son. The churches' answers on the doctrine are on the card below.
r: Genesis 1:1–2; Nehemiah 9:6; John 1:3; Hebrews 11:3; Romans 4:17; Wisdom 11:17; 7:22–23

a: so that in the mercy to come I may receive you back with your brothers
p: The Greek has 'in the mercy', probably the time of God's mercy when the dead are raised.
b: En tō eleei, "in the mercy", is short for the day of God's mercy, when the faithful dead will be raised and families restored. The mother uses the same word in 7:23 ("in his mercy"). It is a mother's hope: not only life after death, but her sons given back to her. The Catechism lists this verse with 7:9 and 7:14 (Catechism 992).
orig: ἵνα ἐν τῷ ἐλέει σὺν τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς σου κομίσωμαί σε (hina en tō eleei syn tois adelphois sou komisōmai se)

a: I am not listening to the king's order. I listen to the order of the law
t: Obeying God rather than the king
p: The youngest son plays on 'listen' and 'obey', the same Greek word. The apostles say the same in Acts 5:29.
b: The Greek plays on hypakouō, "obey", and akouō, "hear, listen". He will not "obey" the king; he "hears" the law. The apostles answered the council, "Obeying God has to come before obeying people" (Acts 5:29). Daniel's three friends had said to Nebuchadnezzar that they would not serve his gods (Daniel 3:16–18). On when believers may refuse rulers, see the card at Esther 3.

a: the servants of Heaven
p: The Greek ouranious paidas can mean 'heavenly servants' or 'children of Heaven', those who belong to God.
b: Paides means both "children" and "servants". The phrase tous ouranious paidas calls the brothers either "the servants of Heaven" (God's servants, as in 7:33) or "heavenly children", those destined for heaven. The KJV has "the servants of God". Since the brothers are young sons, the double sense is likely meant.
orig: ἐπὶ τοὺς οὐρανίους παῖδας (epi tous ouranious paidas)

a: God's covenant of ever-flowing life
p: Aenaos, 'ever-flowing', is a word for springs. The covenant promises life like a spring that never fails.
b: The image recalls God as "the spring of living water" (Jeremiah 2:13) and Jesus' promise of "a spring inside him, of water leaping up into eternal life" (John 4:14). The brothers' short pain is set against life that flows on forever. On the reading "fallen under" or "drunk of", see the variant.

a: I hand over my body and my life for our fathers' laws
p: The verb is used of handing oneself over to death. The New Testament uses the same language of Christ.
b: The youngest son "gives up" (prodidōmi) body and life, as his brothers did. Eleazar wanted his death to be an example (6:28); this son wants his to do something for the nation. Paul writes of "the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me" (Galatians 2:20), and Jesus of coming "to give his life as a ransom in place of many" (Mark 10:45). The comparison was drawn early: see the next note.

a: admit that he alone is God
t: The confession forced on the king
p: The brother prays that the king will confess the one God. In chapter 9 Antiochus does.
b: The prayer echoes the confession of Israel, "the LORD is God. Apart from him there is no other" (Deuteronomy 4:35), and the hope that the nations will know it (Isaiah 45:22–23). It comes true in 9:12–17, where the dying king says it is right to be subject to God and vows to become a Jew. Nebuchadnezzar makes a similar confession after his punishment (Daniel 4:34–37).

a: in me and my brothers
t: Compared with the Bible: the martyrs' deaths for the nation
p: The youngest asks God to stop his anger in him and his brothers. Compare Isaiah 53 and what the New Testament says of Christ.
b: In Swete's text the brothers ask God "to stop" his anger in them (see the variant): God, not the death itself, ends the wrath. The next chapter answers the prayer: as soon as Judas gathers his men, "the Lord's anger had now turned to mercy" (8:5). 4 Maccabees goes further, calling the martyrs "a ransom for the sin of the nation" whose death was an atoning sacrifice (hilastērion, 4 Maccabees 17:21–22; compare 6:28–29). Agrees with the pattern of Isaiah 53: "he was pierced because of our rebellions" (Isaiah 53:5). Goes beyond, or conflicts: the New Testament gives this role to Christ alone, "by one offering he has made perfect forever those who are being made holy" (Hebrews 10:14), and uses hilastērion of him (Romans 3:25). How far other believers' sufferings share in it, the churches answer on the card below.
r: 8:5; Isaiah 53:4–12; Romans 3:25; Hebrews 10:14; Colossians 1:24; 4 Maccabees 6:28–29; 4 Maccabees 17:21–22

a: So this one too died pure
p: Katharōs, 'purely', means he died undefiled by the forbidden food, and with a clean conscience.
b: The adverb katharōs, "cleanly, purely", sums up what all the martyrs died for: they would not be defiled (5:27; 6:19). The KJV has "died undefiled". "Trusting fully in the Lord" gives the reason they could die so.
orig: καθαρῶς μετήλλαξεν (katharōs metēllaxen)

a: the mother met her end
p: The rabbis retold her story under Roman persecution: the Talmud's mother of seven, and Lamentations Rabbah's Miriam.
b: The Talmud tells of "a woman and her seven sons" commanded by "the emperor" to bow to an idol. Each son refuses with a verse of the Torah; the youngest is offered a way out if he will just stoop to pick up the king's ring. His mother tells him to say to Abraham that Abraham bound one son on the altar, but she bound seven. She then falls from a roof and dies, and a heavenly voice quotes "a glad mother of children" (Psalm 113:9) (Bavli Gittin 57b, on Psalm 44:22). Lamentations Rabbah tells it of Miriam bat Nahtom (on Lamentations 1:16). 2 Maccabees does not say how she died; 4 Maccabees 17:1 says she threw herself into the fire.
r: Psalm 44:22; Psalm 113:9; Genesis 22:9; Lamentations 1:16; Jeremiah 15:9; 4 Maccabees 17:1

a: the sacrificial meals
p: The writer closes with the word for eating the sacrificial organs, the act all the martyrs refused.
b: The word splanchnismos (6:7, 21; 7:42) frames the martyr stories: the king's feasts are where faithfulness is tested. In Greek sacrifice the splanchna, heart, liver and lungs, were roasted and shared first among the worshipers. Paul faced the same question in Corinth: "you cannot share in the Lord's table and the table of demons" (1 Corinthians 10:21).
orig: περὶ τοὺς σπλαγχνισμοὺς (peri tous splanchnismous)
